quotes.name: Eleanor Rivera
quotes.quote: From the booth at 19th, on a game day it's not one thing — it's the whole rhythm stacking up. You see the platform fill, and you know the trains are coming, but they're coming full from the last stop. So it's dwell time, sure — people squeezing on, people stepping back, doors cycling. But it's also crowd control, because when the platform's that packed, you're watching for people too close to the edge, and you're holding the train an extra few seconds just to be safe. And honestly, sometimes it's just the sheer number of bodies moving at once — everyone's got somewhere to be, and they all want to be first. That's what explains the gap between how many people we move and how on-time we look. We're moving a lot of people, but moving a lot of people takes time.

quotes.name: Evan Lewis
quotes.quote: I drive the 18 through downtown most evenings, and 19th St has always been the heartbeat stop — folks transferring, heading to work, catching a game. It doesn't surprise me it carries the most people. But I'll tell you, when I pull up alongside that station, I see the crowds waiting and the trains crawling in late, and I think: that's the price of being the busiest. The folks running it, they're doing their best with what they've got — construction everywhere, big events pulling people in. You can't move that many bodies and keep a perfect clock. It's like my route on a game day — you're packed, you're slow, but you're moving people where they need to go. That's the job.
